title: From questions to evidence to a ranked backlog

say: From questions, to evidence, to a ranked backlog.
This is the video for module two of UX Design Fundamentals: research, synthesis and measurement.
Beginners use one method for everything, usually interviews. Professionals start from the research question and pick the method that can answer it.

say: And they measure, because clients trust a redesign far more when you can show numbers than when you say it feels easier.

say: Asking people what they would do and watching what they actually do often give different answers. Both have a place.
Interviews, surveys and open card sorts capture what people say. In a card sort, people group feature cards and name the groups, which shows how they expect things to be organised.

panel.heading: What people say versus what they do

say: Usability tests, analytics and tree tests show what people do. A tree test shows only a text version of your menu, and asks people where they would go to complete a task.

panel.heading: What people say versus what they do

say: For example, Halima is redesigning a cooperative app menu in Kano. One task asks: where would you look to see when your next loan repayment is due?

panel.heading: Tree testing a cooperative app menu
items: Task: find your next loan repayment date

say: 40 people try it. 26 end in the right place, so the success rate is 65%.

panel.heading: Tree testing a cooperative app menu
items: Task: find your next loan repayment date

say: Only 18 got there without going back, so directness is 45%.

panel.heading: Tree testing a cooperative app menu
items: Task: find your next loan repayment date

say: The first clicks explain why. 22 chose Loans, but 12 chose Payments, because they expected a repayment to be a payment.

panel.heading: Tree testing a cooperative app menu
items: Task: find your next loan repayment date

say: So she adds a Loan repayments shortcut under Payments, and retests with 40 new people. 34 succeed, which is 85%. A small cross-link fixed it without rebuilding the app.

panel.heading: Tree testing a cooperative app menu
items: Task: find your next loan repayment date
panel.rule: First clicks explain failures. Fix, then retest with new people.

say: Synthesis turns raw notes into insights. Keep three levels separate.
An observation is what happened, with evidence. For example, 4 of 5 participants paused for over 20 seconds at the BVN field.

cards.d: What happened, with evidence. 4 of 5 participants paused for over 20 seconds at the BVN field.
Why, backed by several observations. Users fear the BVN gives access to their money.
What to change. Explain at the field that the BVN cannot on its own be used to withdraw money.

say: An insight is your interpretation of why: users do not know why the app needs their BVN, and fear it gives access to their money.

cards.d: What happened, with evidence. 4 of 5 participants paused for over 20 seconds at the BVN field.
Why, backed by several observations. Users fear the BVN gives access to their money.
What to change. Explain at the field that the BVN cannot on its own be used to withdraw money.

say: A recommendation is what to change: explain in one line that the number confirms identity and cannot on its own be used to withdraw money.
When grouping notes, count participants, not notes, so one talkative person does not dominate.

say: When you have more ideas than time, score them. RICE multiplies Reach, the people affected, by Impact and by Confidence, then divides by Effort in person-months.

panel.heading: Rank ideas with RICE
items: Reach x Impact x Confidence, divided by Effort

say: For example, Ifeoma scores three ideas. Rewriting the BVN explanation reaches 5,000 users for half a month of effort. It scores 8,000.

panel.heading: Rank ideas with RICE
items: Reach x Impact x Confidence, divided by Effort

say: Saving form progress scores 2,400. A Pidgin option scores 250, because confidence is only 50%, so she plans a survey first.
Scores support judgement. Write down where each number came from, and override openly for legal, safety or accessibility reasons.

panel.heading: Rank ideas with RICE
items: Reach x Impact x Confidence, divided by Effort

say: SUS has 10 statements rated from 1 to 5, given right after a test session. For each odd item, subtract 1 from the answer. For example, participant P2's odd items add up to 17.

panel.heading: Scoring the System Usability Scale
items: Odd items: subtract 1 from the answer
Even items: subtract the answer from 5

say: For each even item, subtract the answer from 5. P2's even items also add up to 17.

panel.heading: Scoring the System Usability Scale
items: Odd items: subtract 1 from the answer
Even items: subtract the answer from 5

say: Add them. 17 plus 17 is 34.

panel.heading: Scoring the System Usability Scale
items: Odd items: subtract 1 from the answer
Even items: subtract the answer from 5

say: Multiply by 2.5. P2's score is 85. The average across many products is about 68, so 85 is well above average. But it is a score, not a percentage.

panel.heading: Scoring the System Usability Scale
items: Odd items: subtract 1 from the answer
Even items: subtract the answer from 5
panel.rule: SUS is a score out of 100, not a percentage. About 68 is average.

say: Tell participants what you study, how answers are stored, and that they can stop at any time. Collect only what you need, under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.
With small samples, report 4 of 5 with a range, not 80% alone. Use median time. Never claim significance from a five-person test. And keep raw data so anyone can check your arithmetic.

panel.heading: Before you report results
items: Consent given; only needed data collected
Small samples: counts plus a range
No significance claims from five people
Raw data kept in a sheet

say: To remember. Start from the question. Report tree tests with success, directness and first clicks. Keep observation, insight and recommendation separate.
Count participants, not notes. And measure the same tasks before and after a redesign.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Start from the question, then the method
Tree tests: success, directness, first clicks
Measure the same tasks before and after
